text: Every other kampong on the mainland is gone, but this one is still here — and as of 2024, the rent for some of its houses is $6.50 a month.
Those figures have barely moved in decades — the same $6.50 to $30 range reported in 2007 and again in 2024 — and if a tenant is short of money, the landlady will take rice or fruit instead.
There are twenty-five families left — twelve Chinese, thirteen Malay — living in wooden houses with zinc roofs along earth lanes, behind the HDB blocks of Buangkok Green.
The landlady is Sng Mui Hong, who was seventy-one when CNA profiled her in November 2024, and who has promised her late father that the kampong will not be sold.
"As long as I have enough to live, that's already fine," she said.
The land — 12,248 square metres of it, roughly three football fields — was swamp when Sng Teow Koon bought it in 1956 from a Mr Huang Yu Tu.
The legal reason: the land was private, bought and paid for, not state land awaiting a plan.
In 2007 the land was reported to be valued at $33 million, and the New Paper put her answer in a headline: "My family ties are not for sale."
She said it herself, the same year: "I can never regain this feeling of simplicity and freedom, and be close to my childhood memories."
Documentary crews, school groups and weekend walkers followed.
The site is divided in the Master Plan into four parcels: a major road toward Seletar, a primary school, a secondary school and a neighbourhood park.

In Parliament on the 2nd of October 2017, MP Intan Azura Mokhtar asked for its preservation; the Second Minister for National Development, Desmond Lee, replied that redevelopment would likely come only "several decades later," tied to the long-term growth of Seletar.
Mohamed Sulaiman, a long-time resident, said at the time: "If government say, can stay, 20 year – I very happy.
I don't know I where, 100 over years already, but if can stay, I happy."
This one survives because a medicine seller bought a swamp in 1956, and because his youngest daughter decided that enough money was enough.

I grew up in Aukang, and most of my life was lived within a few streets of this kampong - in Jalan Payoh Lai, in Jalan Teliti, in Jalan Tari Piring off Jalan Kayu, and in a rented house in Jalan Sindor, off Yio Chu Kang Road.
On my next visit home, I intend to walk it.
